summary: A country on the equator in western Central Africa, about eighty percent covered by tropical rainforest, rich in oil and manganese, and independent from France since 1960.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: In 1844 Spiritan missionaries from France arrived in the area of present-day Libreville to preach; France then gradually colonized Gabon and in 1910 incorporated it into French Equatorial Africa. The Catholic Church ran most of the schools of the colonial period and trained Gabon's first generation of intellectuals and political elite, so it remained the largest church after independence in 1960, with followers throughout the country.

ranking.name: Other Christianity (Awakening churches, etc.)
ranking.description: After Gabon restored multiparty democracy in 1990, religious activity became freer, and the "Awakening churches" (Églises éveillées), which stress the gifts of the Holy Spirit, healing and prosperity theology, appeared in large numbers in the cities, attracting many former Catholics and Protestants. In addition, Bwiti, which blends Christianity with traditional beliefs, also has many followers.

ranking.name: Protestantism
ranking.description: In 1842 American Presbyterian missionaries set up a station near Libreville, one of the earliest Christian missions in Gabon; after 1892 it was taken over by the Paris Evangelical Missionary Society. The hospital that the theologian and physician Albert Schweitzer founded at Lambaréné in 1913 was also connected with this Protestant mission. Protestantism is found mainly among the Fang of the north and in coastal areas, and today's Evangelical Church of Gabon originates from it.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam was brought mainly by West African merchants and migrants from Mali, Senegal, Cameroon and elsewhere, during the colonial period and after independence. President Omar Bongo's conversion to Islam in 1973 drew attention, but native Muslims remain few and the believers are mostly foreign residents.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The non-religious are found mostly in cities such as the capital Libreville, which is related to the spread of education and urban life. Because traditional beliefs and Christianity are often interwoven in daily life, relatively few people identify with no religion at all.

religion.background: The indigenous peoples of Gabon practiced ancestor worship, such as the Fang "Biéri" ancestor cult and the initiation rites of Bwiti. In the mid-19th century American Presbyterian and French Catholic missionaries arrived in turn, and with French colonial expansion Catholicism became the mainstream. After independence in 1960 religious freedom was guaranteed, and after democratization in the 1990s various charismatic "Awakening churches" arose, while traditional beliefs have continued in the form of Bwiti, blended with Christianity; today Christians form an overwhelming majority in Gabon.

ranking.name: French
ranking.description: In 1839 France signed a treaty with coastal chiefs to obtain a foothold, and French was thereafter spread through colonial education and administration; after independence in 1960 it became the sole official language. Gabon has more than forty ethnic groups with different languages, so French became the common language for communication across ethnic lines; young people in the capital Libreville even mostly speak French as their mother tongue, making Gabon one of the African countries with the highest proportion of native French speakers.

ranking.name: Fang
ranking.description: Fang belongs to the Bantu language group and is the language of the Fang, Gabon's largest ethnic group. The Fang migrated in from the north around the 18th–19th centuries and live in the northern provinces of Woleu-Ntem and Estuaire, extending into Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea. The Fang have great political and economic influence, and Fang is the most widely used indigenous language in Gabon.

language.history: Almost all of Gabon's indigenous languages belong to the Bantu group, more than forty in all, including Fang, Punu, Nzebi and Myene, and before colonization the peoples traded with one another along the rivers. In the 15th century Portuguese navigators arrived on the coast, and the name "Gabon" itself comes from Portuguese. From the 19th century French colonization made French the language of education and administration; after independence in 1960 French was made the official language, and in the cities it has gradually replaced the indigenous languages as the everyday language of young people.

ranking.name: Poulet nyembwe (chicken in palm sauce)
ranking.description: Chicken stewed in a thick red sauce made from palm fruit pulp, with onion, garlic and chili added; the flavor is rich and slightly sweet, and it is eaten with white rice or cassava sticks.
ranking.history: "Nyembwe" is the Gabonese word for the palm fruit; the oil palm is native to West and Central Africa and has been an important source of fat there for thousands of years. This dish is regarded as the national dish of Gabon, made with palm fruit that grows naturally in the forest and with poultry, and it represents Gabon's food culture built on forest produce. It often appears at family gatherings, festivals and weddings, and seafood or fish can also be cooked with the same sauce.

ranking.name: Cassava sticks (bâton de manioc)
ranking.description: Cassava is soaked and fermented, pounded into a paste, wrapped tightly in banana or arrowroot leaves into long sticks, and steamed into a springy staple with a slightly sour taste.
ranking.history: Cassava originated in South America and was brought to Central Africa by Portuguese traders via the Atlantic trade in the 16th century; being drought-tolerant and high-yielding, it became the staple of Gabon and the Congo Basin. The practice of fermenting and steaming it in leaves both removes the cassava's toxins and lets the food keep for several days, making it suitable for long journeys and for sale in markets. Cassava sticks are the everyday staple that Gabonese eat with all kinds of stews and grilled fish.

ranking.name: Odika sauce
ranking.description: The kernels of wild mango (Irvingia gabonensis) are roasted and pounded into a block, then grated and cooked into a thick black sauce, often served with fish or meat.
ranking.history: The wild mango from which odika is made has "Gabon" in its scientific name; it is a tree native to the forests of equatorial Africa and has been gathered and used by local people for hundreds of years. The dark brown block pressed from the roasted kernels is nicknamed "Gabonese chocolate" and keeps for a long time. The sauce made with odika is a representative of traditional Gabonese cooking and shows how forest peoples use wild plants.

ranking.name: African plum (atanga)
ranking.description: The fruit of the African plum has a purple-blue skin; after boiling or charcoal grilling, the flesh softens, with a buttery smooth texture and a slight tartness, and it is often eaten with cassava sticks.
ranking.history: The African plum is a fruit tree native to Central Africa, called atanga in Gabon; during the season from about June to September each year, it is sold everywhere in markets and at roadside stalls. People often roast it until soft and eat it with cassava sticks as a simple meal or snack. Because it is widely planted in villages, it has also become an important source of income for many families, and is the taste of the season for Gabonese.

ranking.name: Fried plantain
ranking.description: Ripe plantains are sliced or cut into pieces and fried in oil; the outside caramelizes and the inside is soft and sweet, and it can be a side dish or a snack, often eaten with stewed chicken or grilled fish.
ranking.history: Plantains were introduced to Central Africa hundreds of years ago and widely grown, becoming an important source of starch in Gabon and neighboring countries. Fried plantain is simple to make and very common at street stalls and family tables, often eaten with stewed chicken, grilled fish or beans. It is also a common element of Central African cuisine from before and after colonization, reflecting a diet based on plantain and cassava in the tropical climate.
